title: CUDA Matrix Multiplication
summary: Walkthrough of a tiled CUDA matrix multiplication kernel using shared memory, explaining how patches of A and B are indexed.
body:
• Tiled matrix multiplication
  • Here each thread is responsible for one row of A and one column of B, but it processes that row and column in batches inside the for loop, because shared memory is used
  • When i=0, the first patch is processed; note that tx is the column and ty is the row
if (i*BLOCK_SIZE + tx < numAColumns && row < numARows)
    sharedM[ty][tx] = A[row*numAColumns + i * BLOCK_SIZE + tx];
else
    sharedM[ty][tx] = 0.0;

if (i*BLOCK_SIZE + ty < numBRows && col < numBColumns)
    sharedN[ty][tx] = B[(i*BLOCK_SIZE + ty)*numBColumns + col];
else
    sharedN[ty][tx] = 0.0;
__syncthreads();

  • For example, for the first block of matrix C, at i=0 the threads reach __syncthreads() once the first patches of A and B have been loaded into shared memory; then sharedM and sharedN are multiplied and accumulated, and i=1 is processed next. Note: this is still the first block. One thread handles one row of A and one column of B, and it is now processing the second patch of that row and column; sharedM and sharedN are refilled, and this is the shared memory of the same block

  • Patches are divided along the columns of A, because the number of rows of B equals the number of columns of A

  • A[row*numAColumns + i * BLOCK_SIZE + tx] fetches the value from the corresponding patch of A; here i indexes the columns of A, i.e. which patch along the columns

  • B[(i*BLOCK_SIZE + ty)*numBColumns + col] is different because here i indexes the rows of matrix B, i.e. which patch along the rows

__global__ void matrixMultiplyShared(float *A, float *B, float *C,
    int numARows, int numAColumns, int numBRows, int numBColumns, int numCRows, int numCColumns)
{
    //@@ Insert code to implement matrix multiplication here
    //@@ You have to use shared memory for this MP

    __shared__ float sharedM[BLOCK_SIZE][BLOCK_SIZE];
    __shared__ float sharedN[BLOCK_SIZE][BLOCK_SIZE];

    int bx = blockIdx.x;
    int by = blockIdx.y;
    int tx = threadIdx.x;
    int ty = threadIdx.y;


    int row = by * BLOCK_SIZE + ty;
    int col = bx * BLOCK_SIZE + tx;


    float Csub = 0.0;

    for (int i = 0; i < (int)(ceil((float)numAColumns / BLOCK_SIZE)); i++)
    {
        //printf("block.x=%d,block.y=%d,threadIdx.x=%d,threadIdx.y=%d,row=%d,col=%d,sharedM[%d][%d]=A[%d],value of A: %f,sharedN[%d][%d]=B[%d],value of B: %f\n",
        //	blockIdx.x, blockIdx.y, threadIdx.x, threadIdx.y, row, col,
        //	threadIdx.y, threadIdx.x, row*numAColumns + i * BLOCK_SIZE + tx, A[row*numAColumns + i * BLOCK_SIZE + tx],
        //	threadIdx.y, threadIdx.x, (i*BLOCK_SIZE + ty)*numBColumns + col, B[(i*BLOCK_SIZE + ty)*numBColumns + col]);

        if (i*BLOCK_SIZE + tx < numAColumns && row < numARows)
            sharedM[ty][tx] = A[row*numAColumns + i * BLOCK_SIZE + tx];
        else
            sharedM[ty][tx] = 0.0;

        if (i*BLOCK_SIZE + ty < numBRows && col < numBColumns)
            sharedN[ty][tx] = B[(i*BLOCK_SIZE + ty)*numBColumns + col];
        else
            sharedN[ty][tx] = 0.0;
        __syncthreads();


        for (int j = 0; j < BLOCK_SIZE; j++)
            Csub += sharedM[ty][j] * sharedN[j][tx];
        __syncthreads();
    }


    if (row < numCRows && col < numCColumns)
        C[row*numCColumns + col] = Csub;

}

title: Memoization for Backtracking
summary: How to use a memo keyed by index and depth to avoid repeated searches in backtracking, with a LeetCode Combinations example.
body:
Most backtracking involves some repeated searching; a memo can record earlier search results so you can return directly when you reach the same node

idx is an important index: to its left are idx + 1 ~ n-1 (i = idx + 1, idx + 2 … n-1)

Likewise, the values of i in the subtree of idx are also idx + 1 ~ n-1 (i = idx + 1, idx + 2 … n-1)

  • Therefore, using idx and the depth as the memo key is a good way to store this node

Example

link : https://leetcode.com/problems/combinations/description/

           cout << k << "memo"<<cur;

title: LLTM Gradients
summary: Forward and backward pass of the LLTM PyTorch C++ extension, with notes on deriving the gradients via the chain rule.
body:
• Forward pass
#include <vector>

std::vector<at::Tensor> lltm_forward(
    torch::Tensor input,
    torch::Tensor weights,
    torch::Tensor bias,
    torch::Tensor old_h,
    torch::Tensor old_cell) {
  auto X = torch::cat({old_h, input}, /*dim=*/1);

  auto gate_weights = torch::addmm(bias, X, weights.transpose(0, 1));
  auto gates = gate_weights.chunk(3, /*dim=*/1);

  auto input_gate = torch::sigmoid(gates[0]);
  auto output_gate = torch::sigmoid(gates[1]);
  auto candidate_cell = torch::elu(gates[2], /*alpha=*/1.0);

  auto new_cell = old_cell + candidate_cell * input_gate;
  auto new_h = torch::tanh(new_cell) * output_gate;

  return {new_h,
          new_cell,
          input_gate,
          output_gate,
          candidate_cell,
          X,
          gate_weights};
}
  • Backward pass
// tanh'(z) = 1 - tanh^2(z)
torch::Tensor d_tanh(torch::Tensor z) {
  return 1 - z.tanh().pow(2);
}

// elu'(z) = relu'(z) + { alpha * exp(z) if (alpha * (exp(z) - 1)) < 0, else 0}
torch::Tensor d_elu(torch::Tensor z, torch::Scalar alpha = 1.0) {
  auto e = z.exp();
  auto mask = (alpha * (e - 1)) < 0;
  return (z > 0).type_as(z) + mask.type_as(z) * (alpha * e);
}

std::vector<torch::Tensor> lltm_backward(
    torch::Tensor grad_h,
    torch::Tensor grad_cell,
    torch::Tensor new_cell,
    torch::Tensor input_gate,
    torch::Tensor output_gate,
    torch::Tensor candidate_cell,
    torch::Tensor X,
    torch::Tensor gate_weights,
    torch::Tensor weights) {
  auto d_output_gate = torch::tanh(new_cell) * grad_h;
  auto d_tanh_new_cell = output_gate * grad_h;
  auto d_new_cell = d_tanh(new_cell) * d_tanh_new_cell + grad_cell;

  auto d_old_cell = d_new_cell;
  auto d_candidate_cell = input_gate * d_new_cell;
  auto d_input_gate = candidate_cell * d_new_cell;

  auto gates = gate_weights.chunk(3, /*dim=*/1);
  d_input_gate *= d_sigmoid(gates[0]);
  d_output_gate *= d_sigmoid(gates[1]);
  d_candidate_cell *= d_elu(gates[2]);

  auto d_gates =
      torch::cat({d_input_gate, d_output_gate, d_candidate_cell}, /*dim=*/1);

  auto d_weights = d_gates.t().mm(X);
  # d_gates is the gradient computed from the current cell's operations (e.g. sigmoid); multiplying it by the current input gives the gradient of the full weight matrix
  auto d_bias = d_gates.sum(/*dim=*/0, /*keepdim=*/true);

  auto d_X = d_gates.mm(weights);
  # d_X is the gradient of X
  const auto state_size = grad_h.size(1);
  auto d_old_h = d_X.slice(/*dim=*/1, 0, state_size);
  auto d_input = d_X.slice(/*dim=*/1, state_size);

  return {d_old_h, d_input, d_weights, d_bias, d_old_cell};
}

How to compute d_output_gate (the output_gate gradient) and d_new_cell (the new_cell gradient)

  • Using the chain rule for d_output_gate, let L be the loss.
    The forward pass is:
    auto new_h = torch::tanh(new_cell) * output_gate;
    The backward pass is then:
    d(L)/d(new_h) * d(new_h)/d(output_gate) = grad_h*torch::tanh(new_cell)

  • Similarly, for d_new_cell,
    the forward pass is
    auto new_cell = old_cell + candidate_cell * input_gate;
    auto new_h = torch::tanh(new_cell) * output_gate;
    The backward pass is then:
    d(L)/d(new_h)*d(new_h)/d(new_cell) = grad_h * (d_tanh(new_cell)*output_gate)
    I don't know yet why grad_cell is added here.
    My understanding is that new_cell uses old_cell; it can also be seen as substituting new_cell into torch::tanh(new_cell),

title: GeneralizedRCNN Resize
summary: Notes on NumPy/PyTorch broadcasting rules and how GeneralizedRCNN computes pairwise box overlaps with [:, None] indexing.
body:
GenerlizedRCNN

  • [:, None, None] : Shape [3] -> [3, 1, 1]

  • In NumPy the * operator denotes the element-wise product (multiplying corresponding positions)

    • a = np.array([1,2,3])
    • b = np.array([2,2,2])
    • a * b
    • array([ 2., 4., 6.])

  • For two matrices a and b, compare their dimensions from the last one backwards; broadcasting is possible only if every dimension satisfies one of the following conditions.

    • They are equal

    • One of them is 1

boxes1 # shape[N,4]
boxes2 # shape[M,4]

    lt = torch.max(boxes1[:, None, :2], boxes2[:, :2])  # left-top [N,M,2]
    rb = torch.min(boxes1[:, None, 2:], boxes2[:, 2:])  # right-bottom [N,M,2]
  • Here a dimension is inserted as the second dimension of boxes1, making it [N,1,4], so when it meets boxes2 it is automatically broadcast to [N,M,4]: each row is copied M times (think of them as rows), so every column of boxes1's [:,M,4] is identical, e.g. [1,2,3]->[[1,2,3],[1,2,3]]
  • Broadcasting again, when boxes2 meets boxes1 the last two dimensions are now identical, so boxes2 becomes [N,M,4], which amounts to copying the whole of boxes2 N times
  • So boxes1's [:,M,4] is really just one box's [xmin,ymin,xmax,ymax] repeated M times; essentially there is only one set of coordinates
  • boxes2's [0,:,:] is equivalent to the original boxes2, so this amounts to comparing (computing) the first box's coordinates (row) in boxes1 against all the coordinates in boxes2

title: The Subjunctive Mood
summary: A summary of English subjunctive forms for present, past and future conditions, plus special cases after suggest, wish, it is time and would rather.
body:
1. Subjunctive contrary to present fact:

If + did / were + …, … would/ should/ could/ might + do (base form of the verb)

If I were you, I would go abroad at once. (I am not you.)

If he knew it now, he could help me. (He doesn’t know it now.)

  1. Subjunctive contrary to past fact:

If + had done + …, … would (might) have done …

If I had known your telephone number yesterday, I would have phoned you. (I didn’t know your telephone number.)

If you had come here a little earlier just now, you might have met her. (You didn’t come here earlier.)

  1. Subjunctive contrary to future fact:

(1) If + should + v., … would + v. (very unlikely) (translated as "in case")

If it should rain tomorrow, you could stay at home.

If I should fail, what should Ido?

(2) If + did / were to + v …, would + v. (completely impossible)

If the sun were to rise in the west, I would lend you the money.

If you finished it in 3 minutes, I would give you my car.

  1. Special key points

[Simple memory aids]:

● The "object clause" after the following verbs uses the subjunctive, i.e. should + base form of the verb; should is omitted in American English (a TOEFL grammar point). Common verbs of this kind include: order, ask, decide, demand, require, recommend, suggest, insist (to firmly demand), advise, etc.

He suggested that we (should) help them with English.

The teacher ordered that the homework (should) be finished within half an hour.

● The appositive clause after the following nouns uses the subjunctive "should + base form of the verb" (should can be omitted). Common nouns of this kind include: suggestion, order, request, demand, importance, proposal.

He made a suggestion that we (should) have a fancy dress party.

I think it is a thing of importance that it (should) be done soon.

● It is / was important / necessary / natural / essential / advisable / strange / surprising, etc. + that + subject + should + v.

It is strange that you should say such a thing.

It was important that you should tell me all the information.

● In the object clause after wish and in the adverbial clause after as if, the following subjunctive forms must be used:

subject + wish + (that) + subject + did / were (for the present)

had done (for the past)

would + v. (for the future)

I wish that I met my uncle now.

I wish I had met my uncle yesterday.

I wish I could meet my uncle tomorrow.

● It is (high) time that … + did / were …

It is time that you went to bed.

● would rather that … + did / were …

I would rather that you were not here now.

● would sooner that … + did / were …

I would sooner that you got up earlier.

I would sooner that you were not my brother.

title: Deriving Coordinate Rotation and Translation
summary: Deriving the 2D rigid-body rotation formulas with basic trigonometry, expressing a point in a rotated coordinate frame.
body:
1. How to derive coordinate translation and rotation

The rotation of 2D coordinates can be derived with trigonometric formulas.

In geometric transformations we often need to rotate all the points of a coordinate system; this operation is called a rigid-body rotation (all points rotate while their relative positions stay unchanged). The figure below shows a typical rigid-body rotation in a 2D coordinate system. We rotate the blue coordinate system by θ degrees, and the new coordinate system is the red one. Suppose we know the coordinates of a point relative to the red coordinate system ($x_{red}$, $x_{red}$ ) and the rotation angle θ, and we want to find the coordinates of that point relative to the blue coordinate system ($x_{blue}$,$y_{blue}$)

This is actually simple and can be solved easily with high-school trigonometry. From the figure, the invariant is the length of the black line segment, which we can compute from the coordinates of the black point in the red coordinate system ($x_{red}$, $x_{red}$ ). The length of the black segment is $r=\sqrt {x_{red}^2+y_{red}^2}$

Then, using the purple triangle, we can compute the coordinates of the black point relative to the blue coordinate system ($x_{blue},y_{blue}$)

From high-school trigonometry we know that:
$
x_{blue}=r*cos(\alpha+\theta) \tag{1}
$

$
y_{blue}=r*sin(\alpha+\theta) \tag{2}
$

$\alpha$ is unknown, but we can find a clue about it.

$$
x_{red}=r*cos(\alpha)\\
y_{red}=r*sin(\alpha)
$$

Expanding (1) and (2) gives:

$$
\begin{align}
x_{blue}&=r∗cos(α+θ)=r∗(cos(α)∗cos(θ)−sin(α)∗sin(θ))=x_{red}∗cos(θ)−y_{red}∗sin(θ)\\
y_{blue}&=r∗sin(α+θ)=r∗(sin(α)∗cos(θ)+cos(α)∗sin(θ))=y_{red}∗cos(θ)+x_{red}∗sin(θ)
\end{align}
$$

title: CMake Basics
summary: Notes on CMake: why it exists, make install, CTest tests, configure_file, and embedding the Git hash and build time into a header.
body:
The cmake repository contains some examples from my learning.

1. Why CMake?

There are many Make tools, such as GNU Make, Qt's qmake, Microsoft's MS nmake, BSD Make (pmake), Makepp, and so on. These Make tools follow different specifications and standards, and the Makefile formats they execute vary widely. This creates a serious problem: if software is meant to be cross-platform, it must be guaranteed to compile on different platforms. With the Make tools above, you would have to write a Makefile for each standard, which would be maddening. CMake is a tool designed to solve exactly this problem: it first lets developers write a platform-independent CMakeList.txt file to customise the whole build process, and then generates the required native Makefiles and project files according to the target user's platform.

2. make install

  • Customising the paths of the compiled .o files and .h files

    2.1 CMakeLists.txt in the main directory

    cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 2.8)

project(demo1)
#PROJECT_SOURCE_DIR/CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR/_SOURCE_DIR: the path of the folder containing the nearest CMakeLists.txt file that contains the PROJECT() command.
#PROJECT_BINARY_DIR/CMAKE_BINARY_DIR/_BINARY_DIR: the directory where the cmake command is run, i.e. where the project build takes place.

configure_file(
    "${PROJECT_SOURCE_DIR}/config.h.in"
    "${PROJECT_BINARY_DIR}/config.h"
)
option(USE_MYMATH "Use the provide library" ON)

if(USE_MYMATH)
    include_directories("${PROJECT_SOURCE_DIR}/math")
    add_subdirectory(math)
    set(EXTRA_LIBS ${EXTRA_LIBS} MathFunctions)
endif(USE_MYMATH)

aux_source_directory(. DIR_SRCS)

# Specify the generated exe file

add_executable(Demo1 ${DIR_SRCS})
target_link_libraries(Demo1 ${EXTRA_LIBS})

# Specify the output directories
install(TARGETS Demo1 DESTINATION bin)
install(FILES "${PROJECT_BINARY_DIR}/config.h" DESTINATION include)
    • cmake_minimum_required: the minimum required CMake version
    • project: the project name
    • configure_file: reads the configuration file; just write config.h.in here, and config.h will be generated automatically
    • option: a switch with two values, ON and OFF
    • Variables inside if don't need ${}
    • include_directories: the paths in which to look for header files
    • add_subdirectory: adds a subfolder, which holds some of the classes needed
    • set: assigns the values that follow to the first variable; here:
      • set(EXTRA_LIBS ${EXTRA_LIBS} MathFunctions)
      • EXTRA_LIBS ${EXTRA_LIBS} means: if EXTRA_LIBS already has a value, append to it; otherwise it is empty
      • Same as path=${path}:/usr/
    • aux_source_directory: finds the source files to build in the current folder
    • add_executable: the name of the generated executable
    • target_link_libraries: links the sub-libraries (the functions and classes main needs)
    • install(TARGETS Demo1 DESTINATION bin): the path for the .o files; the default prefix is /usr/local/, so here it is /usr/local/bin
    • You can use set to modify the built-in variable CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX
    • install(FILES “${PROJECT_BINARY_DIR}/config.h” DESTINATION include): the path for the .h files, here /usr/local/include’

    2.2 CMakeLists.txt in the math directory

    aux_source_directory(. DIR_LIB_SRCS)

# Build the MathFunctions library
add_library (MathFunctions ${DIR_LIB_SRCS})
install(TARGETS MathFunctions DESTINATION bin)
install(FILES MathFunctions.h DESTINATION include)

    2.3 Adding tests to the project

    CMake provides a testing tool called CTest. All we need to do is call a series of add_test commands in the CMakeLists file in the project root directory.

    # Enable testing
  enable_testing()

  # Test whether the program runs successfully
  add_test (test_run Demo 5 2)

  # Test whether the help message is shown correctly
  add_test (test_usage Demo)
  set_tests_properties (test_usage
  PROPERTIES PASS_REGULAR_EXPRESSION "Usage: .* base exponent")

  # Test 5 squared
  add_test (test_5_2 Demo 5 2)

  set_tests_properties (test_5_2
  PROPERTIES PASS_REGULAR_EXPRESSION "is 25")

  # Test 10 to the power of 5
  add_test (test_10_5 Demo 10 5)

  set_tests_properties (test_10_5
  PROPERTIES PASS_REGULAR_EXPRESSION "is 100000")

  # Test 2 to the power of 10
  add_test (test_2_10 Demo 2 10)

  set_tests_properties (test_2_10
  PROPERTIES PASS_REGULAR_EXPRESSION "is 1024")

    Or use a macro

    # Define a macro to simplify testing
  macro (do_test arg1 arg2 result)
  add_test (test_${arg1}_${arg2} Demo ${arg1} ${arg2})
  set_tests_properties (test_${arg1}_${arg2}
   PROPERTIES PASS_REGULAR_EXPRESSION ${result})
  endmacro (do_test)

  # Use the macro to run a series of data tests
  do_test (5 2 "is 25")
  do_test (10 5 "is 100000")
  do_test (2 10 "is 1024")

3. configure_file

  • configure_file(input output options)
  • Copies a file (given by the input argument) to the specified location (given by the output argument) and modifies its contents according to options.
  • The configure_file command is generally used for custom build options or custom macros. According to the rules specified by options, configure_file automatically converts the cmakedefine keywords and their contents in the input file.

```
#cmakedefine var3 "${var3}" #Note: the name inside ${} must match the variable name after cmakedefine

```

4. Getting the Git hash and version with CMake: a complete example

GitHub code
Sometimes we need to record information such as the version number, the Git hash and the build time in a project, but obviously we don't want to fill in the Git hash and build time by hand. Here is a way to write this information into a header file and then compile it into a .so library or an executable.

That way, these values can be obtained through an interface provided by the library or from the output printed by the executable.

4.1 The utils.cmake file

```
# Used to get the Git hash and branch
macro(get_git_hash _git_hash)
    find_package(GIT QUIET)
    if(GIT_FOUND)# GIT_FOUND is a built-in variable
        execute_process( # cmake: execute_process runs an external command
            # COMMAND is the command-line command to run
            # GIT_EXECUTABLE is the path to the git executable; -1 means the last commit
            #--pretty=: display commit history in another format; options include oneline, short, medium, full, fuller, email, raw and format:<string>; the default is medium, e.g.:
            # --pretty=oneline: one line per commit, showing only the hash and the commit message (--oneline can also be used as a standalone option)
            # --pretty=format:” ": controls the format of the displayed records, e.g.:
            #     %H  full hash of the commit object
            #     %h  abbreviated hash of the commit object
            #     %T  full hash of the tree object
            #     %t  abbreviated hash of the tree object
            #     %P  full hash of the parent object
            #     %p  abbreviated hash of the parent object
            #     %an author name
            #     %ae author email address
            #     %ad author date (format can be customised with the -date= option)
            #     %ar author date, relative ("how long ago")
            #     %cn committer name
            #         What is the difference between author and committer?
            #         Relationship between author and committer: the author is the one who modified the program, the committer is the one who committed the code (how could someone else pull your changes and commit them if you never committed them yourself?)
            #         In fact, the author is the person who actually made the change, and the committer is the person who finally committed that work to the repository. So when you publish a patch for a project and a core member merges it into the project, you are the author and that core member is the committer (got it)
            #     %ce committer email address
            #     %cd commit date (format can be customised with the -date= option)
            #     %cr commit date, relative ("how long ago")
            #     %s  commit message
            COMMAND ${GIT_EXECUTABLE} log -1 --pretty=format:%h
            OUTPUT_VARIABLE ${_git_hash}        # store the output string in a variable
            # OUTPUT_VARIABLE: specifies the variable that receives what is written to standard output;
            OUTPUT_STRIP_TRAILING_WHITESPACE    # strip the trailing newline from the string
            ERROR_QUIET                         # silence execution errors
            WORKING_DIRECTORY                   # working directory
            ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}
            )
        endif()
endmacro()

# get git branch
macro(get_git_branch _git_branch)   # start of the macro
    find_package(Git QUIET)     # find Git; QUIET suppresses errors
    if(GIT_FOUND)
    execute_process(          # run a child process
        COMMAND ${GIT_EXECUTABLE} symbolic-ref --short -q HEAD
        OUTPUT_VARIABLE ${_git_branch}        # store the output string in a variable
        OUTPUT_STRIP_TRAILING_WHITESPACE    # strip the trailing newline from the string
        ERROR_QUIET                         # silence execution errors
        WORKING_DIRECTORY                   # working directory
        ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}
        )
    endif()
endmacro()                      # end of the macro

```
  • Use macro to define two macros
  • Use execute_process to run external commands
  • OUTPUT_VARIABLE captures what is printed to the command line and assigns it to a variable

title: For vs. Of
summary: Explains when to use the prepositions for and of, covering recipient, purpose, reason and time, with example sentences.
body:
for and of

First, a summary of when to use the prepositions “for” and “of”. “For” is usually used to indicate the recipient, purpose or reason of an action, while “of” is often used to give information related to something. For example, “of” can express attributes or possession between things. In addition, both “for” and “of” can be used to talk about time, but in different ways.

Listen to the first set of examples. Both sentences are about a necklace and use “for” and “of” respectively, but their meanings are completely different.

(Recipient)

  • Was this necklace made for me?
    (Was this necklace made especially for me?)

  • Is this necklace made of gold?
    (Is this necklace made from gold?)

(Purpose)

  • How many grams of soybeans do we need to make tofu? We need thirty grams for tofu.
    (How many grams of soybeans are needed to make tofu? Thirty grams of soybeans are needed for the tofu.)

  • We need thirty grams of tofu.
    (Thirty grams of tofu are needed.)

In the first example, “We need thirty grams for tofu.” means “we need thirty grams of soybeans to make tofu”. Here, “for” indicates purpose. In the second example, “We need thirty grams of tofu.” means “we need thirty grams of tofu itself”; “of” has nothing to do with purpose here and names the thing being measured.

  • This is the house for our clients.
    (This is the house prepared for our clients.) The preposition “for” indicates the use or purpose of the house

  • This is the house of our clients.
    (This is the house that belongs to our clients.) Here, “of” indicates possession.

(Reason)

  • She won an award for her brilliant performance.
    (She received an award because her performance was brilliant.)

  • She won an award of £1000.
    (She received prize money of £1000.)

Both “for” and “of” can be used to talk about time, but in different ways. With time, “for” usually indicates how long something lasts, while “of” tends to introduce what the activity lasting that time is. Listen to the fifth set of examples.

  • I had to listen to him for two hours!
    (I was forced to listen to him talk for two hours!)

  • I had to listen to two hours of him speaking!
    (I was forced to listen to him talk for two hours!)

Both sentences mean “I had to listen to him talk for two hours”, but they use “for” and “of” respectively. In the first sentence, “listen to him for two hours”, “for” indicates how long the act of listening lasted. In the second, “listen to two hours of him speaking”, “of” introduces what exactly those two hours of listening consisted of.

notes

In general, “for” indicates the recipient, purpose or reason of an action, while “of” gives information related to something, such as attributes or possession. When talking about time, “for” usually indicates how long an action lasts, while “of” explains what the action specifically is. It is worth listening to the examples again to consolidate your understanding of the two words.

title: Restrictive and Non-Restrictive Relative Clauses
summary: The six differences between restrictive and non-restrictive relative clauses in English: form, function, translation, meaning, antecedent and relative words.
body:
A restrictive relative clause restricts the meaning of the noun or pronoun it modifies; generally, if the clause is removed, the meaning of the sentence becomes unclear or is even lost. A non-restrictive relative clause is less closely tied to the main clause (the rest of the sentence) and has little effect on the meaning of the noun or pronoun it modifies; if it is removed, the sentence is still complete. It can be thought of as something added on, and it is usually separated from the rest of the sentence by commas. Specifically, restrictive and non-restrictive relative clauses differ in the following ways:

    1. Different form: a restrictive relative clause is not separated from the main clause by a comma, and there is no pause in speech; a non-restrictive relative clause is usually separated from the main clause by a comma, and there is a pause in speech.
    1. Different function: a restrictive relative clause modifies, restricts and identifies the antecedent, and removing it leaves the sentence incomplete or the concept unclear; a non-restrictive relative clause adds supplementary information about the antecedent, and if it is omitted the sentence is still clear and complete: People who take physical exercise live longer.
      Those who exercise live longer. (Without the clause, the sentence loses its meaning.)

His daughter, who is in Boston now, is coming home next week. His daughter is in Boston now and will be back next week. (Without the clause, the sentence is still complete.)

    1. Different translation: when translating relative clauses into Chinese, a restrictive clause is usually placed before the antecedent it modifies, while a non-restrictive clause is translated separately from the main clause: He is the man whose car was stolen. He is the one who had his car stolen.

I’ve invited Jim, who lives in the next flat. I invited Jim; he lives next door.

I invited Jim; he lives next door.

    1. Different meaning. Compare: I have a sister who is a doctor. I have a sister who is a doctor. (I have more than one sister.)

      I have a sister, who is a doctor. I have a sister, and she is a doctor. (I have only one sister.)

    1. Different antecedents: the antecedent of a restrictive relative clause can only be a noun or pronoun, whereas the antecedent of a non-restrictive relative clause can be a noun or pronoun, or a phrase or a whole sentence. In addition, when the antecedent is a proper noun or something else unique:

Peter drove too fast, which was dangerous. Peter drove very fast, which was dangerous. (which refers to drove too fast) He changed his mind, which made me very angry. He changed his mind, which made me angry. (which refers to the whole main clause) Mr. Smith, who is our boss, will leave for Japan Our boss, Mr. Smith, is going to Japan next week. (The antecedent is a proper noun, so a non-restrictive relative clause must be used.)

Her father, who has a lot of money, wishes her to study abroad. Her father is rich and wants her to study abroad. (The antecedent is a common noun with a unique referent, so a non-restrictive relative clause must be used.)

    1. Different relative words: the relative words that and why can be used in restrictive relative clauses but are usually not used in non-restrictive ones; in addition, the relative word can sometimes be omitted in a restrictive relative clause, but it is never omitted in a non-restrictive relative clause.

summary: How to back up and restore a Docker volume, using a MongoDB container and a temporary Ubuntu container.
body:
If a Docker container uses a volume, you need to export the volume’s data, because it is not a bind mount

  • Suppose we first create a mongo container

docker run -p 27017:27017 –name mongo -v mongo-data:/data -d mongo:4.4

mongo-data is a volume mapped to /data, because mongo stores its data under data by default, including db and the configuration files

  • Export (backup): create a new ubuntu container that mounts the same volume as the container to be exported

E.g. the Tower of Hanoi: its subproblems need no combining; all the sub-solutions together form the solution to the whole problem



The subproblems of the Tower of Hanoi are as follows:

- 1) Move N-1 disks to the auxiliary peg
- 2) Move the Nth disk to the target peg
- 3) Move the N-1 disks on the auxiliary peg to the target peg, using the currently free peg.

title: Byte Alignment
summary: The rules of C/C++ struct byte alignment and padding, illustrated by how member order changes sizeof(student) from 16 to 12.
body:
• The starting address of a struct variable is divisible by the size of its widest basic-type member;
  • The offset of each member relative to the struct's starting address is an integer multiple of the member's size; if necessary, the compiler inserts padding bytes between members (internal padding);
  • The total size of the struct is an integer multiple of the size of its widest basic-type member; if necessary, the compiler adds padding bytes after the last member (trailing padding)

For example

struct student
{
    char name[5];
    int num;
    short score;
}

|char|char|char|char|
|char|—-|—-|—-|
|——–int——–|
|–short–|—-|—-|

The data needs only 11 bytes (5+4+2), but because int is 4-byte aligned by default, it is stored at a starting address divisible by 4. That is, if name[5] starts at 0, it occupies 5 bytes, and num starts at byte 8 (offset) (because int is 4 bytes, its starting position must be divisible by 4). So sizeof(student)=16, and a few bytes in between sit idle. This makes it easier for the computer to read and write data quickly; it trades space for time. Its data alignment is shown below:

struct student
{
    int num;
    char name[5];
    short score;
}

num starts at 0, name starts at byte 4 (offset) and takes 5 consecutive bytes, and score starts at byte 10 (offset), so sizeof(student)=12. Its data alignment is shown below:
|——–int——–|
|char|char|char|char|
|char|—-|–short–|

title: Subject Clauses
summary: English grammar notes on subject clauses: introductory words, the formal subject it, and when that can be omitted.
body:
Subject clause: a clause that serves as the subject of a sentence is called a subject clause. It usually comes before the predicate verb of the main clause, or is replaced by the formal subject it, with the clause itself moved to the end of the sentence

Subject clauses use declarative word order; the usual structure is “introductory word + subject + predicate + other elements”;

  1. that

    • That you are coming to London is the best news(relative clause; the relative pronoun can be omitted when it is the object of the clause) I have heard this long time.

      Generally the formal subject it is used in place of the subject, and the real subject is moved to the end

    • It is the best news I have heard this long time that you are coming to London

  2. Introduced by whether

    • Whether they would support us was a problem
    • However, whether such a sense of fairness evolved independently in capuchins and humans, or whether it stems from the common ancestor that the species had 35 million years ago, is, as yet, an unanswered question
      • Two coordinated subject clauses introduced by whether act as the subject of is

  3. Introduced by a connective pronoun

    Example: Whoever is in top form wins the game when two matched players meet. When two equals meet, the bolder one wins.

  4. Introduced by a connective adverb

    Example: How this happened is not clear to anyone. Nobody knows how this happened.

  5. Introduced by what (relative-pronoun type)

    Example: What struck me was that they have all suffered a lot. What impressed me deeply was that they had all been through a great deal of hardship.

2. Subject Clauses and the Formal Subject it

  1. For subject clauses introduced by the conjunction that, the formal subject it is usually used in place of the clause:

Example: That they should refuse to sign the petition required great courage. It took great courage for them to refuse to sign the petition.

  1. For subject clauses introduced by a connective pronoun (or adverb), you can either use the formal subject it in place of the clause or put the clause directly at the start of the sentence:

Example: Whether they would support us was a problem. Whether they would back us was still an open question.

  1. For subject clauses introduced by what (relative-pronoun type), the clause is usually placed directly at the start of the sentence.

Example: What I want to know is this. This is exactly what I want to know.

Sometimes the formal subject can also be used.

Example: It is clear enough what he meant. What he meant is quite clear.

  1. If the sentence is a question, the structure with the formal subject it must be used:

Example: Is it true that he is the girl’s father? Is he really the girl’s father?

3. Omitting the Conjunction that

The conjunction that introducing a subject clause can sometimes be omitted and sometimes not. The rule is: if the that-clause comes at the very start of the sentence, that cannot be omitted; if the that-clause comes at the end of the sentence and the formal subject it is used at the start, that can be omitted:

> Example: That you didn’t go to the talk was a pity. It’s a pity you missed the talk. (that cannot be omitted)

> Example: It was a pity (that) you didn’t go to the talk. It’s a pity you missed the talk. (that can be omitted)

body:
• Omitting that in attributive clauses

  • Omitting who and which in attributive clauses

  • How to tell

    When can the relative pronoun in an attributive clause be omitted

  • An attributive (relative) clause is essentially an adjective that modifies a noun. Looking at the tree structure of the sentence, any attributive clause can be split into two sentences.

eg: The cat that is eating an apple has a cute head.
Split here:

Split here:

summary:

that can be omitted only when it is the object of the clause; otherwise it cannot

The cat that is eating an apple has a cute head.
The cat I bought has a cute head.

Note: this rule also applies to attributive clauses with who and which as the relative pronoun.

eg: The man who once saved my life is speaking.
eg: The man whom you saw on the street once saved my life.

Here who can be replaced by whom because it is the object; going further, whom can be omitted, because this is an attributive clause and whom is its object

eg: The man you saw on the street once saved my life.

How to tell

If the relative pronoun (that, which, who) is directly followed by a verb, it is the subject and cannot be omitted. If it is not followed by a verb, it can be omitted.

eg: The picture which caused the sensation is on exhibition.

(which is directly followed by the verb caused and is the subject of the clause, so it cannot be omitted)

eg: The picture that I drew last year is on exhibition.
(that is not directly followed by a verb, so that can be omitted)

Attributive clauses vs. noun clauses

A noun clause is a clause that functions as a noun in a sentence. A noun clause works like a noun phrase: in a complex sentence it can serve as the subject, object, predicative, appositive, object of a preposition, and so on. Depending on its grammatical function in the sentence, a noun clause is therefore called a subject clause, object clause, predicative clause or appositive clause.

  1. First, an attributive clause has an antecedent, and the antecedent can be put back into the clause to make the clause complete;

  2. Second, a noun clause works like a noun phrase and can serve as the subject, object, appositive, etc. in a complex sentence, with different grammatical functions;

  3. Third, a noun clause is equivalent to a noun, whereas an attributive clause is equivalent to an adjective that modifies or restricts a noun or pronoun;

  4. Fourth, an attributive clause only acts as a modifier, so the sentence is still complete if it is removed, whereas a noun clause is a core part of the sentence and cannot be removed.

title: Adverbial Clauses
summary: Rules for omitting the subject and verb in English adverbial clauses, with example sentences.
body:
Omitting the subject and verb in adverbial clauses follows these principles:

  1. When the subject of the clause is the same as the subject of the main clause, the subject of the clause can be omitted and its predicate verb takes the V-ing form. For example:

    • Although working very hard, he failed in the final exam. (Although he worked very hard）

    • After taking the medicine, she felt much better. (After she took the medicine)

    • If going there by air, we’ll have to pay twice the fare. (If we go there by air)

  2. When the subject of the clause is the same as the subject of the main clause, and the predicate verb of the clause is the linking verb be (or contains some form of be), the subject and be can usually be omitted together.

    • Whenever (she is) free, she often goes shopping. Whenever she has free time, she goes shopping.
    • Work hard when (you are) young, or you’ll regret. If you don't work hard while young, you will regret it in old age.
    • While (he was) a young boy, he was always ready to help others. Even as a child, he was eager to help others.

  3. If the subject of the clause differs from the subject of the main clause but is the same as its object, the subject and be in the clause can also often be omitted. For example:

    • Father advised me not to say anything until (I was) asked.

  4. When the subject of the clause is it, and the predicate verb is be or contains some form of be, it and be can often be omitted together. For example:

    • If (it is) possible, he will help you out of the difficulty. If possible, he will help you get out of the difficulty.

    • You must attend the meeting unless (it is) inconvenient to you. Unless it is inconvenient for you, you must attend this meeting.

With multiple levels of recursion, the human brain cannot simulate the recursive process, so you need a recursion tree

#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;
void recursion(vector<int>& nums,vector<int>& temp,int target, int sum,int count,int& len,int current){
    //The three steps of recursion
    //- Determine the parameters and return value
    //- Determine the termination condition
    //- Write the logic for a single level of recursion
    
    if(sum>=target){
        //This is only reached during recursion
        len = min(len, count);
        return;
    }
    for(int i=current;i<nums.size();i++){
        //Originally 4: first backtrack to 4, and the for loop ends
        //Start the second backtrack, i=3 (at this point sum, count and temp have all removed the i=3 and i=4 cases); after the for, i=4
        // Then sum adds the i=4 case, skipping i=3
        //Then backtrack to i=2; after the for, i=3 (here two levels of recursion stack up again (i=3 and i=4),
        //and for i=3 the value of i=2 is gone because it was backtracked; i=4 is a child node of i=3)
        //Use the recursion tree to analyse the whole recursive process
        count++;
        sum += nums[i];
        temp.push_back(nums[i]);
        recursion(nums, temp,target,sum,count,len,i+1);
        //Backtracking starts here: sum, count and temp are all rolled back, but note that i is not
        sum -= nums[i];
        temp.pop_back();
        count--;    
    }
}
int minSubArrayLen(int s, vector<int>& nums) {  
    int len=999;
    vector<int> temp;
    recursion(nums,temp,s,0,0,len,0);
    if (len==999)
        return 0;
    return len;
}
int main(int argc, const char * argv[]) {
    // insert code here...
    vector<int> nums={1,2,3,4,5};
    int len = minSubArrayLen(15,nums);
    cout << len<<endl;
    return 0;
}

title: Replacing Modulo with Bitwise AND
summary: Shows how a % b can be replaced by the faster a & (b-1) when b is a power of two, with an example.
body:
Since bitwise operations are relatively efficient, in some cases, when b is 2 to the power of n, the following substitution holds:

a % b = a & (b-1)

notes:

  • b must be a power of 2

    This guarantees that b has only its highest bit set to 1 and all other bits 0; after subtracting 1, the high 1 bit is cleared and all lower bits become 1.
    After subtracting one, the highest bit is 0 and all the following bits are 1 (b-1 is the largest possible remainder), so this is equivalent to ANDing the low bits with the original number

For example, 14%8: taking the remainder is equivalent to extracting the low bits, and the largest possible remainder is 7. 14 in binary is 1110, 8 is 1000, and 8-1 = 7 is 0111. Since the low bits are now all 1, ANDing with 14 extracts exactly the remainder held in its low bits

title: Red-Black Trees
summary: The five properties of red-black trees and the insertion cases with recolouring and rotations, plus a summary.
body:
Five Properties of Red-Black Trees

  • Every node is red or black
  • The root is black
  • Null leaves are black (this concerns leaf nodes and nodes of degree one: degree 0 and degree 1)
  • The children of a red node must be black (no simple path from the root to a null leaf contains consecutive red nodes)
  • Every simple path from the root to any null leaf contains the same number of black nodes

Therefore, an all-black path is the shortest, and longest< 2*shortest

Building the Tree

  • 1 A newly inserted node is red; first build the red-black tree using plain binary-search-tree insertion
  • 2 After inserting, recolour and rotate

Cases When Building the Tree (inserted node is red)

  • 1 If the inserted node is the root, simply colour it black
  • 2 If the inserted node is a child and its parent is black, no adjustment is needed
  • 3 If the inserted node is a child and its parent is red (there must be a grandparent, and it is black, because the parent is red), there is also always an uncle (a null leaf counts). If the uncle is red, colour the parent and uncle black, colour the grandparent red-> colouring it red may cause a violation, so treat the grandparent as the newly inserted node and repeat upwards
  • 4 If the inserted node is a child and its parent is red (there must be a grandparent), there is also always an uncle (a null leaf counts). If the uncle is black,
    and the parent P’s value lies between the new node N and the grandparent G (N is on the same side as its parent, e.g. the parent is a left child and N is also a left child, or the parent is a right child and N is also a right child), rotate at G: if the left side is heavy (N inserted into the left subtree), rotate right; if the right side is heavy (N inserted into the right subtree), rotate left (skirt shape), and swap colours: swap the colours of G and P

    Right rotation: make the grandparent the right child of the parent
    Left rotation: make the grandparent the left child of the parent

  • 5 If the inserted node is a child and its parent is red (there must be a grandparent), there is also always an uncle (a null leaf counts). If the uncle is black but N is on the opposite side from its parent, rotate P (in case 4 we rotated G). If the parent is a left child, rotate P left; if the parent is a right child, rotate P right. This brings us back to case 4, so just apply the case 4 method. E.g. if the parent is on the right and N is on the left, rotate right at the parent; now both the parent and N are on the right, and then apply the right-side operation from case 4 above

Summary

  • If the inserted node is the root, colour it black.
  • If the parent is black, just insert.
  • If both the parent and the uncle are red, colour both of them black and the grandparent red, then treat the grandparent as the node being inserted and repeat recursively.
  • If the parent and the inserted node are on the same side, colour the parent black and the grandparent red; both on the left: rotate right, both on the right: rotate left. This is done at the grandparent.
  • If the parent is red and the uncle is black and N is not on the same side as its parent, convert to the same-side case (N on the right: rotate left at the parent; N on the left: rotate right at the parent), then perform step four.

title: Other vs. Others
summary: English grammar notes on the difference between other, others, the other and the others, plus common idiomatic patterns.
body:
Both other and others have an indefinite meaning: other can be followed by a noun it modifies, whereas others cannot be followed by a noun. Their relationship can be described as: others = other + plural noun. Others is usually a pronoun

He never thinks of others. (He never considers other people.)

I don’t like these books. Show me some others. (I don't like these books; show me some more.)

In the first sentence, others = other people, meaning “other people” or “others” in general, referring to everyone else; in the second, others = other books, meaning “other books”.

However, to express a definite meaning, we put the definite article before other and others. Likewise, other can be followed by a noun it modifies, while others cannot be followed by a noun, and the relationship still holds: the others = the other + plural noun. For example:

I started last in the race but I soon caught up with the others. (I was the last to start in the race, but I soon caught up with everyone else.)

Here the others = the other people, meaning “the other people”, where the definite article refers specifically to all the other people taking part in the race.

Note: besides a plural noun, the other can also be followed by a singular noun, in which case it cannot be replaced by the others. For example:

This seat is free; the other seat is taken. (This seat is empty; that one is occupied.)

Common idiomatic expressions

①one...the other means “one ... the other ... (of two)”. For example:

What I say goes in at one ear and out at the other. (What I tell him goes in one ear and out the other.)

②one...the others means “one ... the rest ... (of several)”. For example:

Of their five children, one is in China and the others are abroad. (They have five children; one is in China and the rest are abroad.)

Note: for three items, to say “one ... another ... the remaining one ...”, use one…another…the other [the third…]; for four, use one…another…another [a third]…the other [the fourth, the last].

③some...the others means “some ... the rest ...”. For example:

The search party was divided into two groups. Some went to the right, the others went to the left. (The search party split in two: some went right, the rest went left.)

④some…others means “some ... others ...”. For example:

Some people build while others destroy. (Some people build, while others destroy.)

Note: this structure can also be expressed as some…some. For example:

Some of us agree, some disagree. (Some of us agree, and some of us don't.)

title: Friends in Class Templates
summary: Covers the three kinds of friend declarations in C++ class templates and three ways to define template friend functions.
body:
Friend Template Functions in Class Templates

Three kinds of friend declarations can appear in a class template:
(1) A friend declaration of an ordinary non-template class or function, which grants friendship to that specific class or function.
(2) A friend declaration of a class template or function template, which grants access to all instances of the friend.
(3) A friend declaration that grants access only to a specific instance of a class template or function template.

(1) Ordinary friend:

template<class T>

class A{

   friend void fun();

//...

};
In this example, fun can access the private and protected members of any instance of A

(2) General template friendship

template<class type>

class A{

  template<classT>

   friend void fun(T u);

//...

};

Here the friend uses a template parameter different from the class’s; T can be any valid identifier. The friend function can access the data of any instance of A, whether A’s parameter is int, double or anything else.

(3) Specific template friendship

template <class T> void fun(T,u);//for a specific template friendship, this declaration is required

template<class T>

class A{

   friend voidfun<T>(T u);//this could also be friend void fun<char>(char u);

//...

};

Now fun can only access the data of a specific instance of the class. In other words, only a fun and an A with the same template argument are friends: if fun is called with template argument int, it only has access to A<int>. Of course, the T inside <> in friendvoid fun<T>(Tu); can be any type, such as int, double, etc.

 

 

 

Creating friend functions for a class is easy, but moving to templates tends to produce baffling linker errors.
I am not experienced enough to analyse this, so I will simply introduce two ways to define friend functions for class templates

　　１　Closed form

template< typename T >
class MyClass
{
    friend void function( MyClass< T > &arg )
    {
        
     }
 };　　Key point: the friend function is defined inside the template body.

       ２　Open form
template< typename T >
class MyClass
{
    template< typename C >
    friend void function( MyClass< C > &arg );
 };

template< typename C >
void function( MyClass< C > &arg )
{
    
 }　　Key point: a separate template is declared inside the template body. 
　　
　　3 Tell the compiler that the declared function is a template
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

template < typename T >
class A
{
    friend ostream &operator<< < T >( ostream &, const A< T > & );
 };

template < typename T >
ostream &operator<< ( ostream &output, const A< T > &a )
{
    output << "overload succeeded" << endl;
    return output;
 }

int main()
{
    A< int > a;
    cout << a;
 }Key point: explicitly add the template declaration < T> after the overloaded operator or function name, telling the compiler that the friend function is a template with a matching type.

Recommendations:
If the function should correspond to the type the template is specialized with, use method 3 (explicit template declaration)
If the function should be independent of the template’s specialized type, use method 2 (nested template)
For short inline functions, use method 1

title: Template Specialization
summary: Explains full and partial template specialization in C++, and why function templates use overloading instead of partial specialization.
body:
Full specialization

template <class key>
class hash{}

template<>
class hash<char>{}

template<>
class hash<int>{}

template<>
class hash<long>{
    size_t operator() (const long x){
        return x;
    }
}

cout<< hash<long>() (100);
//first create a temporary object, then call the overloaded ()

full specialization aims to specialize some type.
for example:
this is a function for judging equality of two members

template<class T>
bool Isequal(T& p1, T& p2){
    return p1 == p2;
}

But it doesn’t work for string. We need to override this special type


template<>
bool Isequal<char*> (char* p1, char* p2){    
    return strcmp(p1, p2) == 0;
}
  • A template and its specializations should be declared in the same header file. The declarations of all templates with the same name should come first, followed by their specializations

Note that for a function template you don’t need to write <>

template <class T>
T max(const T lhs, const T rhs){   
    return lhs > rhs ? lhs : rhs;
}

template <>
int max(const int lhs, const int rhs){   
    return lhs > rhs ? lhs : rhs;
}
//This is because the compiler can deduce from the signature int max(const int, const int) that it is a specialization of T max(const T, const T).

Note that if specialization function doesn’t have arguments. It has various interpretation. For example

template <class T>
void f(){ T d; }

template <>
void f(){ int d; }

Here the compiler does not know that f() is specialized from f<T>(), so compilation fails with:

error: no function template matches function template specialization 'f'
In this case we need to explicitly specify the "template argument":

template <class T>
void f(){ T d; }

template <>
void f<int>(){ int d; }

partial specialization

  • arguments (in the number of parameters)
  • range: shrink the range. For example, arbitrary type to pointer (any type becomes any pointer type)

For arguments:

Like full specialization, partial specialization provides a custom template for a set of parameters, but a partially specialized template must be instantiated further before it has a concrete signature. Note that function templates cannot be partially specialized.

template <class T1, class T2>
class A<T1, T2>{
    ...
};
template <class T2>
class A<int, T2>{
    ...
};


Function templates cannot be partially specialized; the following declaration fails to compile:

template <class T1, class T2>
void f(){}

template <class T2>
void f<int, T2>(){}


But functions can be overloaded, so declaring another function template meets the need for partial specialization:

template <class T2>
void f(){}              // Note: there is no "template argument" here

In most cases, overloading function templates covers the need for partial specialization. One exception is the std namespace: std is a special namespace in which users may specialize templates but may not add templates (in fact, adding anything at all is forbidden)

For range:

template <class T>
class A{}
template <class U>
class A<U*>{}
// we limit if the type is pointer thereby goes second class

A<string> a;

A<string*> b;

The point of this design is that when pointers need different handling, this partial specialization is used

title: Template Template Parameters
summary: How C++ template template parameters let a Stack take a container template directly, and why default allocator parameters must be declared.
body:
Templates as template parameters

  • It can be useful to allow a template parameter to be a class template itself. We will continue to use the Stack class template as our example.
template <class T1, template<class T2> 
class Container>

class XCls{

    private:
    Container<T> c;
    public:
    ...
}
template<class T>
using Lst = List<T,allocator<T>>;


XCls<string, Lst> mylst;

Because the second parameter in the declaration of the Stack class template is a type (typename Container), when we define a concrete stack type with Stack<int, std::deque>, the second argument must be std::deque, not std::deque. In this definition we write int twice, and the repetition is unavoidable.

To avoid this repetition, we can make the second parameter of Stack a template itself rather than a concrete type.

template<typename T,
         template<typename> class Container = std::vector>
struct Stack
{
    void push(const T& elem)
    {
        elems.push_back(elem);
    }

    T pop()
    {
        if(empty()) throw std::out_of_range("Stack<>::pop: empty!");

        auto elem = elems.back();
        elems.pop_back();
        return elem;
    }

    bool empty() const
    {
        return elems.empty();
    }

private:
    Container<T> elems;
};

As shown above, the second parameter of the Stack class template becomes template class Container. It is still named Container, but it is now a template that takes one type parameter. Since the name of Container's own template parameter is never used, we can omit it. According to the standard, the keyword before Container here must be class, not typename. Finally, a template template parameter can also have a default value; here we set it to std::vector.

With this definition, we would expect to use Stack like this: Stack<int, std::deque> intStack, but the compiler teaches us a lesson.

In the STL, the std::deque class template is defined with two type parameters: the first is the element type and the second is the allocator type. Although std::deque's second type parameter has a default value, when the compiler substitutes std::deque for Container it matches the parameters strictly and ignores the default value.

So we change the definition of Stack as follows:

template<typename T,
         template<typename Elem, typename Allocator = std::allocator<Elem>> class Container = std::vector>
struct Stack
{
    void push(const T& elem)
    {
        elems.push_back(elem);
    }

    T pop()
    {
        if(empty()) throw std::out_of_range("Stack<>::pop: empty!");

        auto elem = elems.back();
        elems.pop_back();
        return elem;
    }

    bool empty() const
    {
        return elems.empty();
    }

private:
    Container<T> elems;
};

title: Who vs. Whom
summary: English grammar notes explaining when to use who and when to use whom, with example sentences.
body:
What’s different between who and whom

Put simply, use whom—which is a pronoun—when it is the object of a sentence. If you can replace the word with “her,” “him,” or “them” for example, use “whom.” You’ll know when to use “whom” if the pronoun is used in the objective case, or action is being done to the pronoun. Take the sentence:

Whom do you believe?

The sentence may sound pretentious, even snobbish. But it is correct because “whom” is the subject of the infinitive “to,” as well as the object of the sentence as a whole.

Many people thus propose that governments need to tackle this issue by controlling the media, whom they see as responsible for inciting this violence through films and television
(Here whom is the object.)

My father is a doctor whom people trusted.

Who/Whom are you going to invite to your party?
(Here you is the subject.)
i.e. which person are you inviting to your party?

Who/Whom can we turn to in case of an emergence?

i.e. if something happens, whom can we ask for help?

We have no idea who/whom the president will choose to be the new manager.

  • Whether introducing a restrictive or a non-restrictive relative clause, when the antecedent refers to a person, you can use either who (informal) or whom (more formal), as long as it is not the object directly following a preposition:

  • This aspect is discussed further by Crane, who / whom I mentioned earlier. (Crane, whom I mentioned before, discusses this aspect further.)

  • In that year he met Rachel, who / whom he was later to marry. (That year he met Rachel, and later married her.)

Note: when it is the object directly following a preposition, only whom can be used:

  • I met a man with whom I used to work. (I ran into someone I used to work with.)

Incidentally, the same applies when introducing wh-questions. For example:

Whom / Who are you writing to? (Who are you writing a letter to?)

Whom / Who do you like best? (Who do you like most?)

If it is the object immediately following a preposition, only whom can be used, but such expressions are usually found only in more formal styles. For example:

With whom did you go? (Who did you go with?)

whom is used as the object

1.Who is at the door?

2.Whom did you see at the door?

Do you know why the first sentence uses who while the second uses whom? The answer is that who is always used as the subject of a sentence or clause, whereas whom is always used as the object.

In the first sentence above, who is the subject. In the second, you is the subject and whom is the direct object.

1.whom did you recommend for the job?

2.Are there any people whom you would recommend?

Note that in both sentences above, you is the subject, and whom is the object of the verb “recommend”.

title: C++ Notes: Static Members
summary: Why C++ static member variables must be defined and initialised outside the class, and why static functions only access static data.
body:
Static functions can only access static data

Why must static member variables be initialised outside the class?

A static variable belongs to the class, not to an object. If it were initialised inside the class, every new object of the class would reset it to the initial value, which could unexpectedly undo what other objects intended by operating on that static variable
However,
static const int a = 1;
can be initialised inside the class, because const means the variable never changes, so the data in the static memory block is the same for every object

Why can't static members be initialised inside the class?

In C++, a static member of a class must be declared inside the class and initialised outside it, like this:

class A
{
private:
static int count ; // declared inside the class
};

  • Defined and initialised outside the class, without repeating the static keyword
    int A::count = 0 ;
    Or it can just be defined without an initial value, but whether the default is 0 probably depends on the compiler?

  • Defined only, without an initial value; the default value depends on the compiler
    int A::count;
    Why?

  • Because a static member belongs to the whole class rather than to any particular object. Initialising it inside the class would mean every object contains that static member, which is a contradiction.

Without int A::count = 0 ; // variable definition, compilation will fail with an “undefined reference to ‘A::count’” error. This is because the static member variable count has not been defined, i.e. no memory has been allocated for it yet, so it obviously cannot be accessed.

title: Shallow and Deep Copy in C++
summary: Explains shallow versus deep copying of classes with pointer members in C++, with a copy-constructor example.
body:
Shallow copy and deep copy
Shallow-copying a pointer causes heap data to be freed twice
Problem: While running algorithm experiments recently, I ran into a problem with assigning class pointers. A simple assignment between pointers just makes both point to the same address, but I needed to push_back the class pointer after each run of the algorithm into a vector to store the result of every iteration. If the same pointer were stored every time, all the class pointers in the vector would point to the same address. This made me wonder whether class pointers could be assigned so that the two have the same contents but point to different addresses, i.e. they are two distinct pointers.

Definitions

Shallow copy: as I understand it, data members are assigned from one object to another. For simple data types a shallow copy is perfectly adequate, but when there are pointers, a shallow copy between two objects makes their pointers point to the same address, and an error occurs when the destructors run (the same pointer is freed twice).

Deep copy: builds on the shallow copy but handles the pointer copying so that the pointers inside the two objects point to different regions; the two objects have the same contents but are stored in different areas of memory.
‘’’
class rect
{
public:

rect();
rect(const rect *r);
~rect();

private:
int width, height;
int *p;
};
rect::rect(const rect *r)
{
width = r->width;
height = r->height;
p = new int;
*p = *(r->p);
}

rect::rect()
{
p = new int(100);
}

rect::~rect()
{
if (p != NULL)
delete p;
}
int _tmain(int argc, _TCHAR* argv[])
{
rect *rect1;
rect *rect2;
rect1 = new rect;
rect2 = new rect(rect1);

return 0;

}
‘’’
Both the class pointers and the member pointer p now point to different addresses

title: Why the Assignment Operator Returns a Reference
summary: Explains shallow copy, overloading operator= in C++, and why it returns a reference to support chained assignment.
body:
If a user-defined class does not overload its = operator, the compiler generates one automatically. However, this compiler-generated overload may be unsafe, because it performs a so-called “shallow copy”: for a pointer, it copies the pointer's value rather than the memory it points to. The memory then has two pointers pointing to it, and the class objects are destructed twice, but the memory can only be freed once, so the second free causes an access error.

　　To avoid this “shallow copy” problem, you need to overload the = operator. It is a binary operator, so the function name and parameters are easy to determine; the key point is its return type. Generally, it should return a reference to the class type, so that so-called “chained assignment” works. The question I once had was: why must it return a reference to enable “chaining”? Here I think it through and summarise, starting from the code.

Copy code
class Student
{
public:
Student(const char* name);~Student();
Student& operator=(const Student &student);private:
char *m_name;
};
Copy code
Copy code
//Test code
Student s1(“Lee”);
Student s2(“Diwen”);
Student s3(“Tom”);

//First s2 = s1 is executed, i.e. s2.operator=(s1), which returns a reference to s2
//Then s3 = s2 is executed, i.e. s3.operator=(s2)
s3 = s2 = s1;
Copy code
　　Chained = is evaluated from right to left. So the right-hand side certainly has to return an object of type Student. The question is: why return a reference?

　　Look at the function that overloads the = operator: its parameter type is a const reference, meaning the argument passed in must be an lvalue. If the return type were Student, it would return an anonymous object (an rvalue); in chained assignment this return value (an rvalue) must in turn be passed in as an argument, which obviously would not work (it doesn't work without const, but does with const).
A const reference can bind to an rvalue, and the overloaded assignment operator returns a reference, of course, to avoid a pointless copy.

title: Processes and Threads
summary: Explains the differences between processes and threads using a train-and-carriages analogy, including mutexes and semaphores.
body:
A simple analogy: process = train, thread = carriage. Threads run within a process (
a carriage on its own cannot move). A process can contain multiple threads (a train can have multiple carriages)
Data is hard to share between different processes (passengers on one train find it hard to switch to another train, e.g. when transferring at a station)
Data is easy to share between threads of the same process (moving from carriage A to carriage B is easy)
Processes consume more computer resources than threads (running several trains costs more than adding several carriages)
Processes do not affect one another, but one thread crashing brings down the whole process (one train does not affect another, but if a carriage in the middle of a train catches fire, all its carriages are affected)
Processes can scale out to multiple machines, while threads are at most suited to multiple cores (different trains can run on multiple tracks, but carriages of the same train cannot run on different tracks)
Memory addresses used by a process can be locked, i.e. when one thread is using some shared memory, other threads must wait until it is done before using that memory (like the toilet on a train) — “mutex”. Memory addresses used by a process can be limited in how many may use them (like the dining car on a train, which only lets in a certain number of people; if it is full, you wait at the door until someone comes out) — “semaphore”

title: In-Class Declaration and Definition
summary: Explains defining C++ member functions inside versus outside the class, implicit inlining, and when inlining is not worthwhile.
body:
1. In-class definition

    What in-class definition means: the body (implementation) of a member function is written inside the class. C++ implicitly treats such functions as inline.

   A.h

class A
{
public:
A(void);
virtual ~A(void);
int test(){return 1;};
int test1();
};
As you can see, the member function test() of class A is defined inside the class, so it is implicitly inline. (Inlining trades space for time: at the cost of duplicating code, it only saves the overhead of the function call, thereby improving execution efficiency. If executing the code in the function body takes much longer than the call overhead, the gain is small. So inlining is not appropriate when the function body is long or contains loops, if or switch statements, or recursion.)

2. Out-of-class definition

   What out-of-class definition means: the member function is defined outside the class, like the member function test1() in class A, which only has a declaration inside the class.

   A.h

class A
{
public:
A(void);
virtual ~A(void);
int test(){return 1;};
int test1();

Tags: QT  qt  string  linux

1. Cause of the error and how to fix it
When running on Linux and compiling with g++, the code below produces the error: invalid initialization of non-const reference of type ‘std::string&’ from a temporary of type ‘std::string’.

In other words, a non-const reference cannot be initialized from a temporary. That is, the error occurs during argument passing. The offending code is as follows

void print(string& str)
{
cout<<str<<endl;
}
//Calling it like this triggers the error described above

print("hello world");


The cause of the error is that the compiler constructs a temporary string object from the string ”hello world”, and this temporary object is const. When the temporary is passed to a non-const string& reference, the error occurs because binding a non-const reference requires the object to be non-const as well, while here the temporary string object is a const object. The fix, therefore, is to change the parameter of print() to a const reference. With the code modified as follows, it compiles successfully.

void print(const string& str)
{
    cout<<str<<endl;
}
//Compiles successfully
print("hello world");
This code also illustrates a C++ programming principle advocated in Effective C++: use const whenever possible. Doing so makes code more robust and exposes errors at compile time.

2. Are all temporary objects const?
Why must a temporary object be passed as a const reference when used as a reference argument? Many people explain that temporaries are constants that cannot be assigned or modified, so the compiler reports an error when they are passed as non-const references. This explanation works for understanding why temporaries cannot be non-const reference arguments, but it is not precise. Some even go further and claim that all temporary objects are const. So we should approach opinions and resources found online with caution and healthy scepticism, following the "take what is useful" approach advocated by Lu Xun: refer to them and learn from them critically.

In fact, a temporary can be used as an lvalue (LValue) and assigned to; look at the following code:

class IntClass{
private:
    int x;
public:
    IntClass(int value):x(value){
    }

    friend  ostream& operator<<( ostream &os, const IntClass &intc);
};

//Overload the output operator<<
ostream& operator<<( ostream &os, const IntClass &intc)
{
    os<<intc.x;
    return os;
}

//Print function
void print(IntClass & intc)
{
    cout<<intc<<endl;
    //Modify this temporary object through the reference
    intc=8;
    cout<<intc<<endl;
}

int main(int argc,char* argv[])
{
    print(IntClass(6));
}
Program output:
6
8

The code above compiles and runs correctly without errors. IntClass(6) creates an unnamed temporary object, which is passed to a non-const reference, and the print function modifies this temporary through the reference. This shows that not all temporary objects are const.

So which temporaries are const and which are not? Here is a quote found online: "Temporaries of built-in types are const, whereas temporaries of user-defined types are not." I think this explains why the temporary in question can be used as an lvalue.

int* const a = new int;
Here the pointer a itself cannot be modified, e.g. a = &b; is an error
const int* a = new int; int const* a = new int; These two are the same; look at where const is placed
Here the content pointed to by a cannot be modified, e.g. *a = 2; is an error

title: Hierarchical Clustering
summary: Explains hierarchical clustering and compares single, complete and average linkage for measuring distances between clusters.
body:
Hierarchical clustering algorithms and the various linkages

Basic principle
Given N objects to be clustered and an N*N distance matrix (or similarity matrix), the basic steps of hierarchical clustering (see S.C. Johnson in 1967) are as follows:

  1. Assign each object to its own cluster, giving N clusters, each containing just one object. The distance between clusters is the distance between the objects they contain.

  2. Find the two closest clusters and merge them into one, so the total number of clusters decreases by one.

  3. Recompute the distances between the new cluster and all the old clusters.

  4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until everything has been merged into a single cluster (containing all N objects).

    Depending on how step 3 is done, hierarchical clustering methods can be divided into several types: single-linkage, complete-linkage and average-linkage clustering, among others.

Single-linkage clustering (also called the connectedness or minimum method):

The distance between clusters equals the minimum distance between objects in the two clusters; if similarity is used instead, it is the maximum similarity between any object in one cluster and any object in the other.

Complete-linkage clustering (also called the diameter or maximum method):

The distance between groups equals the maximum distance between objects in the two groups.

Average-linkage clustering:

The distance between groups equals the average distance between objects in the two groups.

A variant of average-link clustering is R. D’Andrade's (1978) UCLUS method, which uses the median distance; it is somewhat more robust than the average distance to the influence of outlying data objects.

This kind of hierarchical clustering is called the “agglomerative” method, because it iteratively merges all the clusters. There is also a “divisive” hierarchical clustering method, which works the other way round: it first puts all objects in a single cluster and keeps splitting it into smaller clusters. The divisive method is rarely used.

The whole clustering process actually builds a tree. During construction, a threshold can be set in step 2: when the distance between the two closest clusters exceeds this threshold, the iteration can stop. The other key step is step 3; there are quite a few ways to measure the similarity between two clusters. Three are introduced here:

SingleLinkage: also called nearest-neighbor. It takes the distance between the two closest samples of the two clusters as the distance between the two sets; in other words, the smaller the distance between the two closest samples, the greater the similarity between the two clusters. It tends to cause what is called the Chaining effect: two clusters that are clearly far apart “overall” get merged just because a few of their points are close together, and after such a merge the chaining effect grows further, eventually producing rather loose clusters.

CompleteLinkage: this is the exact opposite extreme of Single Linkage. It takes the distance between the two farthest points of the two sets as the distance between them. Its effect is also the opposite: it is very restrictive. Even if two clusters are already very close, as long as there are uncooperative points, it stubbornly refuses to merge them, which is not a great approach either. The common problem with both of these similarity definitions is that they only consider certain particular data points and ignore the overall characteristics of the data within each cluster.

Average-linkage: this method takes the pairwise distances between all points in the two sets and averages them, which gives relatively more reasonable results.

A variant of average-linkage takes the median of the pairwise distances, which, compared with the mean, does a better job of removing the interference of individual outlying samples.
